full_text:
Interviewer:	How are getting on at the placement then?

Subject:	It’s not too bad

Interviewer:	Are you enjoying it?

Subject:	Hmm most of the time

Interviewer:	OK when did you start?

Subject:	September, 

Interviewer:	And you finish in September is that right? Ok, can you tell me a little about the company that your working for?

Subject:	Hmmm [company] hmm do missile systems (inaudible) launching, the missiles themselves and do all the design work and that.

Interviewer:	OK and how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Hmm there isn’t really a specific attitude to it; it’s just treated like everyone else 

Interviewer:	Yeah? I’ll come back to that one later. How useful do you think that your degree course has been so far to the work that you’re doing?

Subject:	Hmm because it’s a lot of design work hmmm its not really doing much for my first two years cos’ it was doing the equations and the big theory (Yeah) Cos’ at the moment I’m working with future concepts so it’s a lot of just blocking out, so it’s more common sense and being able to use the CAD package, rather than actually doing anything from the course.

Interviewer:	OK is there anything that you wish you had learnt on the course before you started the placement?

Subject:	Hmm not really, no.

Interviewer:	Ok were you taught anything about health and safety at university?

Subject:	No 

Interviewer:	Have you had to do anything about health and safety since you’ve started the placement?

Subject:	Hmm we had to, on our induction we did hmm an hour on health and safety with videos and things and if I go into any of the labs and stuff I have to be sent on hmm various courses relevant to wherever I’m going.

Interviewer:	Ok do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for the placement at all?

Subject:	Not really no.

Interviewer:	Ok before you started did the university or your department say what they hoped you would gain from the placement?

Subject:	Hmm kind of, cos’ hmm engineering run the DIS, they said what they’d like us to get out of it and basically refer this to hmm the IMechE stuff, for what you should do when your doing industrial training (Yeah) It’s not really very specific, its kind of task orientated, its sort of you will be something where you will do a presentation, you will do something where you do do a drawing or a model so.

Interviewer:	Ok did you find that helpful at all or not?

Subject:	Hmm it doesn’t really make much difference cos’ my company run that anyway.

Interviewer:	Yeah OK

Subject:	So, yeah 

Interviewer:	How have you found the transition from education to work - was it easy or difficult?

Subject:	Hmm not too bad, hmm I mean apart from the commuting, it’s sort of still fairly regular.

Interviewer:	Yeah how far are you commuting everyday then?

Subject:	Hmm 20 minute drive.

Interviewer:	Ok have you had to face any new issues at all since you’ve started work?

Subject:	Hmm I’ve had to deal with a lot of hmm, because we work with [organisation] a lot of the security clearance issues and, and commercially sensitive things. A lot of stuff I do, hmm I’ve got to be very wary of who I'm talking to about it, and things like that. 

Interviewer:	Is that difficult getting used to that then?

Subject:	Hmm at the moment its not really difficult, its getting a bit harder now because for the DIS I’ve got to do a dissertation and every time people keep bringing forward titles for me to do, there’s always but you’ve, you cant do this one because that ones secret, this is commercially sensitive you cant do that, you can do this one but you aren’t allowed to refer to x, y and z on it, they must be referred to as this hmm because people shouldn’t know, it’s just getting a bit complicated. 

Interviewer:	Yeah ok, do you feel like the educational experience reflects what its like in industry at all, like what your taught and how your taught? Or they two totally different situations?

Subject:	They are fairly different I mean, currently when I’m doing my stuff its like if there’s anything which is vaguely off and very narrow focused, I get told to speak to so and so or someone else instead of having to do everything and hmm I think at uni cos’ you’re trying to learn everything is very much and you do all this, and here’s a project which is meant to be real life industry stuff, you’ve got to do all this, we don’t have anyone for you to talk to specifically about any of this and all the rest of it and just have to do it myself.

Interviewer:	Yeah, whereas in industry you can go and speak to specialists?

Subject:	Its much more relaxed, its kind of, oh you’ve done that, you wouldn’t have done that, we’ve got, were gonna give it to them anyway and their going to do this for us and so. You don’t need to bother doing that on your drawing because we send it to these people, its like ok.

Interviewer:	OK how do you feel about going back to uni when you’ve finished the placement?

Subject:	Hmm kind of looking forward to it, hmm because I’m, and future concepts, I’m learning a lot more wider focused because next year is the first year we can start picking our optional subjects. Its kind of giving me a lot of focus on what I want to do next. So I mean we’re looking at loads of new processes and I’m being brought into optical engineering and things like that and next year I think I’ve got an option for optical engineering and things like this which I can kind of see where I want to go. 

Interviewer:	OK do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

Subject:	Hmm, not really, industry just has extended goals whereas at uni its very much, you’ve done this and your finished this task, fine, you hand it in, its gets marked, you finish this task, it either goes off somewhere else or you continue it on and you’ve always got to be more aware of, someone’s got to produce it down the line, especially with what I’m doing now, where its just like, oh we can build this on the bench top but we’ve got to be aware that we need to do this because you need to test it in the factory and then you’ve got to build it but you don’t this and then its got to do these tests and you’ve got to be thinking about the whole lot from the start rather than saying sort of this is about the manufacturing tasks, you have these tools, build this, or sort of just design this or do these drawings. Its hmm seeing it all the way through, and being in a position where six months later someone might come back to you and say, you know those things you did, could you just clear this up and actually having to know about it instead of putting it in a drawer and forgetting about it.

Interviewer:	Yeah ok, how big are the company that you’re working for?

Subject:	Hmm it’s the second largest missile company in the world I think. So its hmm its fairly large, its based mainly in [town], where I am, but its also got hmm places in Italy and France and their looking to take it somewhere in Germany. So they’re a fairly large company cos’ they’re linked with [company] and hmm [company] which I cant remember who they are now but hmm yeah there’s lots of large stockholders for us so.

Interviewer:	OK do they employ many women?

Subject:	Hmm I don’t know, in my office there’s a least three other engineers who are women.

Interviewer:	Yeah out of how many?

Subject:	Hmm on my floor there’s probably about 100 but then don’t, because it is all, its like your swiping in everywhere, I don’t see a lot of people. But I know this year they took on three graduates and one of them was a girl, they’ve taken on two undergraduates and it’s me and another guy from here. (Yeah) So they, it doesn’t look to be discriminating against us or anything like that and its never ever been pointed out, I mean [name] whose just finished her graduate training and become an engineer there hmm she’s never had any problems or anything and she thinks its great hmm she sees it as an advantage cos’ although everything else is created like normally, you have more options to, cos’ we hmm they do a lot of WES stuff and SET point stuff, so you have more opportunities to go out because everybody’s on a big drive to get more women in, so more chance to go out and sort of be in the community, you could get out of the office so, that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK do the company have a structure or programme in place for placement students?

Subject:	Yeah they follow the IMechE chartership so, wont have them this year, if I get asked back it will be on the graduate programme, you do two years and you do at least four placements, your around a lot and then after that hmm you get, they’ll give you I think it’s project manager is where a lot of placement programmes have gone and you do that hmm for two years get your charter ship and then they follow you all the way through, they have mentors for you and hmm buddies and all the rest of it to guide you through the whole lot. 

Interviewer:	OK do you get targets set or anything like that while you’re on the placement?

Subject:	Hmm we have development reviews every four to six weeks where they look at, which you and your line manager and you look at tasks which could be coming up seeing how they relate to the IMechE stuff and if its there it’ll be put down to you, your going to do this and set those objectives, but equally if you’ve done stuff which you haven’t thought about over the last development meeting or if things haven’t worked out, it just gets altered around.

Interviewer:	Do you think that sort of thing is a good idea or could it be improved at all?

Subject:	Hmm it’s a bonus because of the DIS and the IMechE thing cos’ whether you were going to go for chartership or not, they still want you to do the same course hmmm, the placements are great cos’ you just get to see everything, and it, I mean I’ve had a really good placement, Andy hmm he’s been put in a different placement and he’s ended up doing a lot different jobs because they haven’t had the work for hmm for a new person so he’s had a hard time, he knows that after Christmas he’s moving on somewhere else. So at least he knows where he doesn’t want to go if he comes back and things like this.

Interviewer:	Do you get to move round areas as well then? OK what does your job role in the company involve?

Subject:	At the moment hmm I’m a design engineer on a seeker project, but I’m also doing bits and pieces on hmm other, [name] another project so.

Interviewer:	Is what are you doing on the placement what you expected or were you told to expect?

Subject:	I wasn’t really expecting anything, cos’ I knew it was a placement so I didn’t know where I was going or anything like that. Hmm I was meant to be part of the seeker unit hmm and most of the work is mainly doing change notes and things so just maintaining records. Hmm but they’re just at the end of the project and didn’t really need me, so I’ve kind of been on loan and doing anything that’s going and [name] he thinks I can do, so I’ve been put in a good position.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility then?

Subject:	Hmmm yeah, its hmm, its good cos’ I keep hmm, cos’ I've ended up doing a lot of design work myself, especially on this last piece and being responsible for a lot of it but hmm cos’ it’s a very small team I've always got my line manager and then the head of department coming up checking me so, but even though it is a lot of work and it is a lot of responsibility, their always checking up yeah.

Interviewer:	Ok how would you summarise the placement experience so far then?

Subject:	Hmmm

Interviewer:	Has it been a positive experience?

Subject:	Hmm definitely, hmm cos’ it is future concepts, I’m learning a lot. I’ve seen a lot things I haven’t seen before, I mean hmm you know you don’t really go to university, see about infra red optic strings and things and hmm yeah, I’m getting a lot out of it cos’ I’m having to do a lot of research as well as design, and a lot of design is off my own back, it’s a case of you go and sort this out and then when your done we’ll see what it is. (Yeah) So its, I don’t know its confidence building rather than technically difficult at the moment, so it is really good. I’m dreading the idea that they might actually ask me to do something technical and I not have clue, but its good cos’ I’m sort of learning a lot and being able to just get on with it and do the work, its sort of, see what people think.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what would you say have been the best and worst things about it so far?

Subject:	Hmm the best is being involved in a new project from the go and being able to see everything and because it’s a small team, it is seeing everything. I’ve been out to visit other companies, hmm other branches of the same company to talk to specialists and hmm all of this. Hmm the worst bit is probably because it is concept work, it tends to be, you have a lot of work and then it suddenly drops off because your missing x, y and z information and you have to wait for a week to find out, so you have a week where you can’t really do anything and your sort of twiddling your thumbs and then it suddenly ramps all over again. So it’s just the workflow is just strange instead of being used to, you’ve got task one, task two, task three and you carry on.

Interviewer:	OK is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

Subject:	Hmm, not really but that’s more because I didn’t really set out to achieve anything, it was a case of I’m doing this placement, we’ll go and we’ll see what its like cos’ if its bad I know where I don’t wanna go, if its good, great. Hmm, especially with other placements I’ve found over the summer when I did hmm things like [company] where they took me on because they wanted to advertise to graduates rather than they had work for me to do and they had some (inaudible) where I just got really bored with it all and really didn’t want to be there. So I sort of did that myself, sort of set myself thinking just in case it turned out to be as bad as previous times so hmm yeah.

Interviewer:	OK you said that it has been confidence building, do you think that it has changed you personally doing the placement?

Subject:	Hmm its made me better at networking if nothing else because I have been sent out to see x, y and z about separate things, even if I think I can do them, talk to these people cos’ they’ve been doing it for years and they might know, and a lot of it is, oh so and so worked on that seven years ago, or something stupid and so you go and have a chat to him and see if he’s got any paperwork lying around from then and all the rest of it, hmm so I’m a lot happier in sort of going out and seeing people whereas at university I was very much I don’t know, so I’ll sit with my text book and I’ll try and work it out and sort it out and get it done, off. Its finished, rather than sort of going out and finding, even if its not to find help its to find more information cos’ these guys have been working on it, most of them working on it for like twenty, thirty years, so even if they don’t the answer, they might know someone who does, and if they aren’t quite sure, you’ll still learn a load about the history of the product or the company or, or that or [name] whose just left and he would have known or things like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that will change your attitude when you come back to uni then?

Subject:	Hmm yeah, it, well. Sort of the last year it was very much, so much work I mean sit down, do it and making myself learn it to do it, rather than going out and saying actually could you explain all this. It was very much more, sort of we’re just going to sit down, we are going to learn this, and we’re not going to go until we’ve learnt it. Hmm so, it will give me a bit more help and sort of know to go out, ask people and try and find out stuff hmm before trying to sit down and driving myself mad over something I don’t quite know on things like this.

Interviewer:	OK what would you now say are the benefits of doing a placement?

Subject:	Hmm well the experience hmm with engineering in particular it’s a year off chartership if you want to do that. Hmm it’s a break from uni instead of being sat with books, going to lectures, having to sit there for two hours and concentrate, its being able to actually do work. If you aren’t happy with something you can go and say I don’t know or I can’t do this and be given something else if things are too much and just actually work through things.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

Subject:	Hmm the only kind of drawback I’ve had is hmm ringing up my friends at school and uni, cos’ all of them are doing three year courses. They’ll have graduated by the time I come back. Hmmm which is kind of rough, hmm trying to come back here and find places to live and stuff, but apart from that hmm, no, if you’ve got a placement you enjoy its fine. From previous experience, if your in somewhere you really don’t like, your kind of stuck there till the end of the year, even if you do say, sort of I don’t like this, you end up going around everywhere and finding out that you really don’t like the company or you don’t like these people, you do have to stay there for a year. Hmm and its very disheartening going to a placement and finding out you really don’t like them and you sit there thinking, I’ve just spent two years doing this degree, I’ve done a job of it and I really hated it, what should I be doing now, and again that can be a positive, if you find out, it’s better to find out after two years that you really should be doing something else than it is to do four years, then you come out and find that you cant try something else or see what else is going on.

Interviewer:	OK I think you said there’s another placement student, do you think it’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having a student on placement with you?

Subject:	Hmm for me its been an advantage because I started a week after him because of re-sits. Hmm so having somewhere, especially cos’ he’s from the same course, hmm knowing somewhere there just give me the sort of to say, tell me where the photocopier is, without having to like go over to your boss on things you should really know and things like that. But the graduate students, hmm are really good as well because they know we’re all in the same boat and a lot of them are doing placements and graduate placements so its kind of, they’ve got the hmm YPA, the Young People’s Association there so everyone kind of looks after everyone else anyway and all the graduates all help you out. Hmm there’s a big system where there’s a list of people with placements they’ve done so if your, find yourself working on a project someone has been and your having trouble with it, you can go to talk to them if you think you need to know something and don’t want to sort of harass your boss with things so. It’s all good.

Interviewer:	OK do you think that the placement students are treated equally?

Subject:	Hmm I think so cos’your, especially with ours where were moved around a lot, it tends to be the line manager, if you’re in the same place as someone was three months ago, you’ll probably be treated the same way. Hmm but then equally if you don’t end up in the same place its all up to the line manager and how they work.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you feel like your treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

Subject:	Hmm I don’t know (laughs) cos’ I’m kinda of on my own cos’ I am like on loan to someone else rather than actually part of the department. Hmm I tend to spend a lot of my time at a desk on my own and a lot of future concept people work on their own anyway, so we’re all spread out. So your kind of left to your own devices and sort of occasionally people can come over and talk to you so I don’t really know.

Interviewer:	OK you’ve just said that most of the work that you do is on your own, have you had to be involved in any team or group work at all?

Subject:	Hmm not yet because of the nature of the project. Hmm there’s only kind of three people working on it and we’re kind of borrowing other people. Hmm [name] and [name] hmm I normally see them everyday and we do a bit of work, but most of it is generally hmm me doing the design work, [name’s] project manager so he’s doing a lot of the research for it and [name’s] technologist so he’s off doing strange things, he talks to us about and we have no idea. So hmm it tends to be very separate, but if I ever need help, they’re both there and they both check up on me and keep an eye so its all good but its not really the group effort on any of it but then there’s people who hmm are on [name] which is a huge project and they’ll be doing, all their work as part of the group and have six meetings a day or having to stay until 8 o clock at night because got people (inaudible) and all the rest of it, working together to try and get something finished. So it just depends where you end up.

Interviewer:	Yeah, will you have the opportunity to be involved with things like that later on?

Subject:	Hmm I hope so, hmm my project, placements are meant to be three months, hmm but I’m spending one for six on my current placement because it is a new project and hmm there’s a lot more to learn cos’ their all doing proto-typing and things like that so I’m staying where I am and hopefully cos’ it is continuing and we’ve got funding more people will come on so, it will become more of a team work whereas before it was kind of can we feasibly do this, put this together?

Interviewer:	OK you mentioned about mentors earlier, have you been given a mentor in the company?

Subject:	Yeah 

Interviewer:	And how do you feel about that?

Subject:	Hmm I don’t know, my mentors worked out a bit strange because he’s actually the head of [name] so he’s my department head as well, so my mentor meetings kind of merge with my development reviews hmmm, so I tend to use my buddy a lot for help and talking about how everything goes cos’ hmm everyone’s assigned, like somebody whose recently graduated or is on the graduate scheme to kind of help them along, and working at the company so I tend to use them instead of my mentor because its not really separated and its not really, I cant really, if I really wanted to, I couldn’t say anything to nasty about the company because but equally, its, even if I do really need time to change, he’s in a position where he can.

Interviewer:	OK so the buddy system is someone that’s more equal to you rather than a mentor, ok, what do you think the role of a mentor is?

Subject:	Hmm just to keep an eye, someone to hmm get feedback off them about what your doing, how you can do stuff, if you want to do hmm a certain course, if you were thinking about, for your next placement you would like to do this and this and just to bounce ideas from if you need it to get information from. 

Interviewer:	So is your buddy doing the same sort of work as the mentor then?

Subject:	Hmm I think a buddy’s meant to be more so that you know someone in the company you can like, take you to lunch and stuff while you get settled, but because of everyone’s so close and everyone looks after everyone, you can get all the same information out of them, or they’ll tell you who you need to talk to.

Interviewer:	OK do you think that the mentee has a particular role to play, if that’s a word?

Subject:	Hmm I don’t know, probably just looking for places to be able to sort of develop yourself, its kind of the buzz phrase, personal development at [company], cos’ they have got a learning development centre, spent lots of money on it, as they keep telling us where they do lots of courses and if you want to do a course which isn’t there, they’ll give you a £100 towards the course and things like that if you want to so hmm at least this company is kind of what they want the mentees to be doing. They want them to be looking to develop themselves instead of being told that you should do this and you should do that.

Interviewer:	OK have you ever been given any bad advice by your mentor or buddy?

Subject:	Hmmm not yet.

Interviewer:	Good. Is there anyone in the company who you think of as a role model?

Subject:	Hmm not really cos’ everyone’s doing such different things, and we’re still kind of learning our way around and even within the company its quite separated because hmm it was such a large company, its like the whole [name] group have only being in [town] for a year cos’ they’ve been in [place] so their kind of linked with everyone else whose had to come up with them and things like that and there’s various places where (inaudible) [town] has adopted everyone. So it’s a bit strange.

Interviewer:	OK what sort of characteristics do you think would make a good role model?

Subject:	Hmm, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	OK that’s ok, have you had anyone from university been to visit you?

Subject:	Yes [name] came up.

Interviewer:	Is that your personal tutor or a placement tutor?

Subject:	He’s my personal tutor and my placement tutor.

Interviewer:	OK, did he explain what the purpose of the visit was?

Subject:	Hmm yeah it was just to check that we were following the DIS properly, to check that we weren’t having too many problems, which couldn’t be sorted out. 

Interviewer:	Did he speak to your line manager as well?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	OK hmm would you be happy to go to him if you did have a problem, any problems?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	Are you in contact with him at other times, can you email him and things like that if you had a problem or would you email anyone else at university?

Subject:	Hmm no I generally email [placement tutor] if there’s a problem and he’ll hmmm put me through to ever needs hmm to know about it, to try and sort it out. 

Interviewer:	OK do you know if either the company or the university have a complaints procedures if there were any problems?

Subject:	Hmm I don’t about the university; hmm at work we do have a general complaints procedure, I got a booklet on it (laughs).

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s a good idea to know about things like that?

Subject:	Hmm probably, if your having problems its always, even if your not, its nice to know that if you do have problems, there’s somewhere you can go and talk about it and sort it out.

Interviewer:	Ok are there appropriate facilities for women at your organisation?

Subject:	 (Laughs) yes

Interviewer:	Can you think of any occasions where you feel like your gender’s determined reactions you’ve got or the outcome of particular events?

Subject:	Hmm not really, the only thing is that all the men there still apologise when they swear but that’s about it, everything else I think.

Interviewer:	Yeah so does that bother you at all when they’re swearing and stuff?

Subject:	It doesn’t bother me, it annoys me when they feel they have to apologise every time cos’ its kind of, I can swear as well. (Yeah) Not doing anything horrible, just get on with it.

Interviewer:	Yeah ok, do you think that you still want a career in engineering then?

Subject:	Yeah 

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will go into the field that you’ve been working in at the minute?

Subject:	Hmm how do you mean what field?

Interviewer:	Well if the company offered you a job when you graduated would you take it?

Subject:	Hmm yeah I’d kind of like to stay in the defence and just kind of I mean I grew up on [area] where sort of [company] and [company] and the rest of it are based and I’ve kind of had it drummed into me if you were doing engineering you should be working for these people, so I’d kind of like to stay there. Hmmm especially if I ended up doing the same work I’m doing now cos’ I’m really happy with it and find it really interesting.

Interviewer:	OK what sort of role do you think that you would like in the future, do you think you’d like to go into the more managerial or more specialist side of things?

Subject:	Hmm I don’t know about specialist cos’ I haven’t done enough places to know (Yeah what…) What I’d like to do, hmm cos’ I feel now if I wanted to be specialist, I’m going to specialise in [name] and its not really thing about [name] or [name]. It’s not really that good.

Interviewer:	So you haven’t got enough experience?

Subject:	Hmmm I’d like to still be involved in projects rather than hmm the managerial aspect because as far as I see, as far up you go, the further you get away from actual engineering you end up probably better off with a business degree or with human resources.
Interviewer:	 (Inaudible)

Subject:	I quite like the distils, have to model stuff up if I have to and things like that.

Interviewer:	OK do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all as a result of doing the placement?

Subject:	Hmm not really, its kind of firmed up what I want to do cos’ I’ve always wanted to do over research or something hands on and I’d like the idea I’m doing a research based placement. Hmm but and as I said I’ve had bad experience placements before and it has made me sit and think maybe I should just become an accountant, because it has just been sitting there brain numbingly boring, filling in paper work or changing a picture by two millimetres, not really being told where and why, just getting it on the desk and you will do this, and its kind of, I didn’t want to do this, I wanted to do engineering because its meant to be sort of hands on and dealing with this or doing some research and looking at stuff. Hmm so it’s kind of given me confidence back into, it can’t all be like this, it’s just a bad experience and I’ll carry on and it’ll be fine, I’ll do my placements and it will all be fine. It’s kind of done my placement, yeah its great, I definitely want to be here, I’m definitely at the right place, there’s no humming and arring about it. 

Interviewer:	Yeah so it’s kind of encouraged you again? 

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work when you finished university?

Subject:	Hmm yeah, it will give me some idea of how I need to operate in a working environment rather than hmm than what I do at uni and just be sort of used to the, that routine and knowing that its all right to know that you need these equations but you’ve got to be able to apply them for this and while your applying it to that, that maybe the optimal answer for that, you need to build it which you can’t do with this and things like that. So just knowing the whole process and I mean if I do end up going back to the same company, it gives me a head start, cos’ I’ll know people there, I already know that if I need help with this, I can go and talk to Mike, or I can talk to John if I need things so.

Interviewer:	Is there any way they could make the course more about the whole process and more hands on?

Subject:	Hmm not really cos’ of, well I don’t know about the second year, where they could probably do more project base work which I know they do anyway, but I mean I don’t know whether it was industrial type project or here’s a work bench, here’s a thousand pounds, build this and sort it out and write a report. Hmm but I don’t think they could in the first year because there’s just so much theory to learn about the background of everything. If you try to make it fit together with a more industrial kind of feel, you never get as much information across, hmm 

Interviewer:	Would you recommend other students do a placement?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	Do you think that it should be compulsory?

Subject:	No because hmm I know a few people who, they’ve decided to carry on with the degree for various reasons, I mean some of them just want to be out of university so they don’t have a stall in their studying, or they’ve taken a year out before they’ve come to uni and don’t want to lose any more time, don’t want to sort of finish and be twice as long to everyone else in university. Hmm as well as people who have done placements before they’ve come here and already know, I think its just kind of the in thing about how, how do you learn and whether you need to sort of know for sure that you want to be on this degree and all the rest of it.

Interviewer:	OK I’ve just got a couple of questions to ask you which I asked you in your last interview to see if your opinion has changed since working in the industry. What five words would you now use to describe your field of engineering? … Shall I tell you what you said last time and see if you still agree? 

Subject:	OK

Interviewer:	You said that it was routed in old ways and well established.

Subject:	Hmm don’t know

Interviewer:	Would you still agree with that?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s a bit strange, never mind. 

Interviewer:	OK do you now think that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	Hmm not really, you’ve just got to get used to, well its more not you getting used to it, its everyone else getting used to you. Hmm it’s more just being able to get on where, sort of guys who have been working their for 30 years and haven’t worked with a girl before. Most of them, their all right, some of them a bit strange about it, just because they are not used to it and sometimes they feel they’ve got to be nice to you and all the rest of it. But as long as you sort of stay acting like you normally act and all the rest of it then they normally get the message that you aren’t to be treated with kitten gloves and all the rest of it, you can do as much as they can, its all fine. 

Interviewer:	Yeah, have your colleagues taken a while to get used to you then?

Subject:	Hmm where I am at the moment, not many people are too bothered, but hmm a lot of the graduates are working with [name] at the moment which is a fairly young team as the company goes and hmm I mean the [name] guys, they don’t teach, they all have teenage daughters and their all about my age and their all (inaudible), get on with it, we know you can do x, y and z, you know you can be as stroppy as anyone else, as long as you don’t sort of go out there thinking that your going to get special treatment or try and get special treatment, its all fine.

Interviewer:	OK do you think that it is an issue that there are say fewer women than men there?

Subject:	I think its become an issue because people have suddenly noticed, hmm in my mind I’ve never seen it as when people have said but you’re a girl, it’s a bit of a strange degree. Its like, I wanted to take the degree, I was interested in it so I’m becoming an engineer. It’s never been kind of, what can I do to, cos’ it will be strange, sort of, I’ll go and be an engineer. I’ve never seen that, its kind of like, yes I’ve done physics and all the rest of it, so I’m doing this, the same way my friends did this and decided they wanted to be doctors or chemistry students, there’s, I just don’t see why its become so (inaudible), its only become a big deal because they’ve looked at their statistics and gone, do you realise that only like 2% of them are women, its like, does it matter as long as the jobs get done and no ones been turned away on purpose because of it. If there’s like actual discrimination, to say no, we only employ blokes, that’s fine, there’s an issue there, but with the whole industry as an employer of women, why does it need to employ women, it needs to employ engineers. (Yeah) So I’m not really into the getting more women into engineering, I’ve always been, if I’ve done stuff with schools and stuff, I don’t mind helping them getting into science and maths and sort of take that kind of route, but in the end I’m not gonna say, oh you really like physics, your good at maths well, come and do engineering, you don’t want to do physics, you don’t want to do anything else, you don’t want to go off and be a doctor, come and do engineering cos’ its great. I’d much rather say well if you like it, get on with it and have a look at what you can do because I don’t see the point in suddenly going, you’ve kind of got the right things, you do want to do this because we need to boost the numbers for whatever reasons. 

Interviewer:	OK that’s great. Just one last thing, you mentioned that another team was much younger than, do you think when people aren’t used to maybe having women to work with, that there is an age issue there? 

Subject:	Hmm I don’t think its so much an age issue, its just what people are used to hmm I mean at lancing, where I did my first placement while I was at A levels hmm although I wasn’t working on the shop floor, I spent a lot of time around fitters, and when they haven’t been around hmm working with women and stuff, they found it quite hard to adjust, but they were kind of more asking lots of questions about why you were there rather than making it any harder for you or anything and stuff. (Yeah) Hmm but then again here, where people from, where people have graduated recently with more women in classes, their fine with that, their used to working with it or at the other end of the scale within my group where there’s people, they’ve got their kids which are as old as I am and know that sort of we’re not going to be (inaudible) and all the rest of it and we don’t need treating with kitten gloves, we can just get on with it, and then there’s people whose sort of have worked a lot with people in HR where it’s the complete reverse, where there’s hundreds of women, not many blokes and their fine with it. But you’ve got people who have come up various companies and they’ve never had any women it’s a bit of a culture shock some of them. Its, its just getting used to things, if you suddenly sort of, I mean I know going from an all girls school in sixth form we were suddenly joined with [school] and it was odd having classes with blokes but after the first month or so you got used to it. (Yeah) It’s just sort of…

Interviewer:	Making more (inaudible)

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	OK that’s everything, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK is there anything that you wish you had learnt on the course before you started the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not really, no.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had to do anything about health and safety since you’ve started the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for the placement at all?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok did you find that helpful at all or not?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How have you found the transition from education to work - was it easy or difficult?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not too bad, hmm I mean apart from the commuting, it’s sort of still fairly regular.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah how far are you commuting everyday then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm 20 minute drive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok have you had to face any new issues at all since you’ve started work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I’ve had to deal with a lot of hmm, because we work with [organisation] a lot of the security clearance issues and, and commercially sensitive things. A lot of stuff I do, hmm I’ve got to be very wary of who I'm talking to about it, and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that difficult getting used to that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm at the moment its not really difficult, its getting a bit harder now because for the DIS I’ve got to do a dissertation and every time people keep bringing forward titles for me to do, there’s always but you’ve, you cant do this one because that ones secret, this is commercially sensitive you cant do that, you can do this one but you aren’t allowed to refer to x, y and z on it, they must be referred to as this hmm because people shouldn’t know, it’s just getting a bit complicated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah ok, do you feel like the educational experience reflects what its like in industry at all, like what your taught and how your taught? Or they two totally different situations?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They are fairly different I mean, currently when I’m doing my stuff its like if there’s anything which is vaguely off and very narrow focused, I get told to speak to so and so or someone else instead of having to do everything and hmm I think at uni cos’ you’re trying to learn everything is very much and you do all this, and here’s a project which is meant to be real life industry stuff, you’ve got to do all this, we don’t have anyone for you to talk to specifically about any of this and all the rest of it and just have to do it myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, whereas in industry you can go and speak to specialists?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Its much more relaxed, its kind of, oh you’ve done that, you wouldn’t have done that, we’ve got, were gonna give it to them anyway and their going to do this for us and so. You don’t need to bother doing that on your drawing because we send it to these people, its like ok.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK how do you feel about going back to uni when you’ve finished the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm kind of looking forward to it, hmm because I’m, and future concepts, I’m learning a lot more wider focused because next year is the first year we can start picking our optional subjects. Its kind of giving me a lot of focus on what I want to do next. So I mean we’re looking at loads of new processes and I’m being brought into optical engineering and things like that and next year I think I’ve got an option for optical engineering and things like this which I can kind of see where I want to go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, not really, industry just has extended goals whereas at uni its very much, you’ve done this and your finished this task, fine, you hand it in, its gets marked, you finish this task, it either goes off somewhere else or you continue it on and you’ve always got to be more aware of, someone’s got to produce it down the line, especially with what I’m doing now, where its just like, oh we can build this on the bench top but we’ve got to be aware that we need to do this because you need to test it in the factory and then you’ve got to build it but you don’t this and then its got to do these tests and you’ve got to be thinking about the whole lot from the start rather than saying sort of this is about the manufacturing tasks, you have these tools, build this, or sort of just design this or do these drawings. Its hmm seeing it all the way through, and being in a position where six months later someone might come back to you and say, you know those things you did, could you just clear this up and actually having to know about it instead of putting it in a drawer and forgetting about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah ok, how big are the company that you’re working for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm it’s the second largest missile company in the world I think. So its hmm its fairly large, its based mainly in [town], where I am, but its also got hmm places in Italy and France and their looking to take it somewhere in Germany. So they’re a fairly large company cos’ they’re linked with [company] and hmm [company] which I cant remember who they are now but hmm yeah there’s lots of large stockholders for us so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do they employ many women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I don’t know, in my office there’s a least three other engineers who are women.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah out of how many?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm on my floor there’s probably about 100 but then don’t, because it is all, its like your swiping in everywhere, I don’t see a lot of people. But I know this year they took on three graduates and one of them was a girl, they’ve taken on two undergraduates and it’s me and another guy from here. (Yeah) So they, it doesn’t look to be discriminating against us or anything like that and its never ever been pointed out, I mean [name] whose just finished her graduate training and become an engineer there hmm she’s never had any problems or anything and she thinks its great hmm she sees it as an advantage cos’ although everything else is created like normally, you have more options to, cos’ we hmm they do a lot of WES stuff and SET point stuff, so you have more opportunities to go out because everybody’s on a big drive to get more women in, so more chance to go out and sort of be in the community, you could get out of the office so, that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do the company have a structure or programme in place for placement students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah they follow the IMechE chartership so, wont have them this year, if I get asked back it will be on the graduate programme, you do two years and you do at least four placements, your around a lot and then after that hmm you get, they’ll give you I think it’s project manager is where a lot of placement programmes have gone and you do that hmm for two years get your charter ship and then they follow you all the way through, they have mentors for you and hmm buddies and all the rest of it to guide you through the whole lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you get targets set or anything like that while you’re on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm we have development reviews every four to six weeks where they look at, which you and your line manager and you look at tasks which could be coming up seeing how they relate to the IMechE stuff and if its there it’ll be put down to you, your going to do this and set those objectives, but equally if you’ve done stuff which you haven’t thought about over the last development meeting or if things haven’t worked out, it just gets altered around.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that sort of thing is a good idea or could it be improved at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm it’s a bonus because of the DIS and the IMechE thing cos’ whether you were going to go for chartership or not, they still want you to do the same course hmmm, the placements are great cos’ you just get to see everything, and it, I mean I’ve had a really good placement, Andy hmm he’s been put in a different placement and he’s ended up doing a lot different jobs because they haven’t had the work for hmm for a new person so he’s had a hard time, he knows that after Christmas he’s moving on somewhere else. So at least he knows where he doesn’t want to go if he comes back and things like this.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get to move round areas as well then? OK what does your job role in the company involve?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At the moment hmm I’m a design engineer on a seeker project, but I’m also doing bits and pieces on hmm other, [name] another project so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is what are you doing on the placement what you expected or were you told to expect?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I wasn’t really expecting anything, cos’ I knew it was a placement so I didn’t know where I was going or anything like that. Hmm I was meant to be part of the seeker unit hmm and most of the work is mainly doing change notes and things so just maintaining records. Hmm but they’re just at the end of the project and didn’t really need me, so I’ve kind of been on loan and doing anything that’s going and [name] he thinks I can do, so I’ve been put in a good position.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmmm yeah, its hmm, its good cos’ I keep hmm, cos’ I've ended up doing a lot of design work myself, especially on this last piece and being responsible for a lot of it but hmm cos’ it’s a very small team I've always got my line manager and then the head of department coming up checking me so, but even though it is a lot of work and it is a lot of responsibility, their always checking up yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok how would you summarise the placement experience so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmmm

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has it been a positive experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm definitely, hmm cos’ it is future concepts, I’m learning a lot. I’ve seen a lot things I haven’t seen before, I mean hmm you know you don’t really go to university, see about infra red optic strings and things and hmm yeah, I’m getting a lot out of it cos’ I’m having to do a lot of research as well as design, and a lot of design is off my own back, it’s a case of you go and sort this out and then when your done we’ll see what it is. (Yeah) So its, I don’t know its confidence building rather than technically difficult at the moment, so it is really good. I’m dreading the idea that they might actually ask me to do something technical and I not have clue, but its good cos’ I’m sort of learning a lot and being able to just get on with it and do the work, its sort of, see what people think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what would you say have been the best and worst things about it so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm the best is being involved in a new project from the go and being able to see everything and because it’s a small team, it is seeing everything. I’ve been out to visit other companies, hmm other branches of the same company to talk to specialists and hmm all of this. Hmm the worst bit is probably because it is concept work, it tends to be, you have a lot of work and then it suddenly drops off because your missing x, y and z information and you have to wait for a week to find out, so you have a week where you can’t really do anything and your sort of twiddling your thumbs and then it suddenly ramps all over again. So it’s just the workflow is just strange instead of being used to, you’ve got task one, task two, task three and you carry on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, not really but that’s more because I didn’t really set out to achieve anything, it was a case of I’m doing this placement, we’ll go and we’ll see what its like cos’ if its bad I know where I don’t wanna go, if its good, great. Hmm, especially with other placements I’ve found over the summer when I did hmm things like [company] where they took me on because they wanted to advertise to graduates rather than they had work for me to do and they had some (inaudible) where I just got really bored with it all and really didn’t want to be there. So I sort of did that myself, sort of set myself thinking just in case it turned out to be as bad as previous times so hmm yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK you said that it has been confidence building, do you think that it has changed you personally doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm its made me better at networking if nothing else because I have been sent out to see x, y and z about separate things, even if I think I can do them, talk to these people cos’ they’ve been doing it for years and they might know, and a lot of it is, oh so and so worked on that seven years ago, or something stupid and so you go and have a chat to him and see if he’s got any paperwork lying around from then and all the rest of it, hmm so I’m a lot happier in sort of going out and seeing people whereas at university I was very much I don’t know, so I’ll sit with my text book and I’ll try and work it out and sort it out and get it done, off. Its finished, rather than sort of going out and finding, even if its not to find help its to find more information cos’ these guys have been working on it, most of them working on it for like twenty, thirty years, so even if they don’t the answer, they might know someone who does, and if they aren’t quite sure, you’ll still learn a load about the history of the product or the company or, or that or [name] whose just left and he would have known or things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that will change your attitude when you come back to uni then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm yeah, it, well. Sort of the last year it was very much, so much work I mean sit down, do it and making myself learn it to do it, rather than going out and saying actually could you explain all this. It was very much more, sort of we’re just going to sit down, we are going to learn this, and we’re not going to go until we’ve learnt it. Hmm so, it will give me a bit more help and sort of know to go out, ask people and try and find out stuff hmm before trying to sit down and driving myself mad over something I don’t quite know on things like this.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what would you now say are the benefits of doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm well the experience hmm with engineering in particular it’s a year off chartership if you want to do that. Hmm it’s a break from uni instead of being sat with books, going to lectures, having to sit there for two hours and concentrate, its being able to actually do work. If you aren’t happy with something you can go and say I don’t know or I can’t do this and be given something else if things are too much and just actually work through things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm the only kind of drawback I’ve had is hmm ringing up my friends at school and uni, cos’ all of them are doing three year courses. They’ll have graduated by the time I come back. Hmmm which is kind of rough, hmm trying to come back here and find places to live and stuff, but apart from that hmm, no, if you’ve got a placement you enjoy its fine. From previous experience, if your in somewhere you really don’t like, your kind of stuck there till the end of the year, even if you do say, sort of I don’t like this, you end up going around everywhere and finding out that you really don’t like the company or you don’t like these people, you do have to stay there for a year. Hmm and its very disheartening going to a placement and finding out you really don’t like them and you sit there thinking, I’ve just spent two years doing this degree, I’ve done a job of it and I really hated it, what should I be doing now, and again that can be a positive, if you find out, it’s better to find out after two years that you really should be doing something else than it is to do four years, then you come out and find that you cant try something else or see what else is going on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK I think you said there’s another placement student, do you think it’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having a student on placement with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm for me its been an advantage because I started a week after him because of re-sits. Hmm so having somewhere, especially cos’ he’s from the same course, hmm knowing somewhere there just give me the sort of to say, tell me where the photocopier is, without having to like go over to your boss on things you should really know and things like that. But the graduate students, hmm are really good as well because they know we’re all in the same boat and a lot of them are doing placements and graduate placements so its kind of, they’ve got the hmm YPA, the Young People’s Association there so everyone kind of looks after everyone else anyway and all the graduates all help you out. Hmm there’s a big system where there’s a list of people with placements they’ve done so if your, find yourself working on a project someone has been and your having trouble with it, you can go to talk to them if you think you need to know something and don’t want to sort of harass your boss with things so. It’s all good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you think that the placement students are treated equally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I think so cos’your, especially with ours where were moved around a lot, it tends to be the line manager, if you’re in the same place as someone was three months ago, you’ll probably be treated the same way. Hmm but then equally if you don’t end up in the same place its all up to the line manager and how they work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you feel like your treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I don’t know (laughs) cos’ I’m kinda of on my own cos’ I am like on loan to someone else rather than actually part of the department. Hmm I tend to spend a lot of my time at a desk on my own and a lot of future concept people work on their own anyway, so we’re all spread out. So your kind of left to your own devices and sort of occasionally people can come over and talk to you so I don’t really know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK you’ve just said that most of the work that you do is on your own, have you had to be involved in any team or group work at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not yet because of the nature of the project. Hmm there’s only kind of three people working on it and we’re kind of borrowing other people. Hmm [name] and [name] hmm I normally see them everyday and we do a bit of work, but most of it is generally hmm me doing the design work, [name’s] project manager so he’s doing a lot of the research for it and [name’s] technologist so he’s off doing strange things, he talks to us about and we have no idea. So hmm it tends to be very separate, but if I ever need help, they’re both there and they both check up on me and keep an eye so its all good but its not really the group effort on any of it but then there’s people who hmm are on [name] which is a huge project and they’ll be doing, all their work as part of the group and have six meetings a day or having to stay until 8 o clock at night because got people (inaudible) and all the rest of it, working together to try and get something finished. So it just depends where you end up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, will you have the opportunity to be involved with things like that later on?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I hope so, hmm my project, placements are meant to be three months, hmm but I’m spending one for six on my current placement because it is a new project and hmm there’s a lot more to learn cos’ their all doing proto-typing and things like that so I’m staying where I am and hopefully cos’ it is continuing and we’ve got funding more people will come on so, it will become more of a team work whereas before it was kind of can we feasibly do this, put this together?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK you mentioned about mentors earlier, have you been given a mentor in the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And how do you feel about that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I don’t know, my mentors worked out a bit strange because he’s actually the head of [name] so he’s my department head as well, so my mentor meetings kind of merge with my development reviews hmmm, so I tend to use my buddy a lot for help and talking about how everything goes cos’ hmm everyone’s assigned, like somebody whose recently graduated or is on the graduate scheme to kind of help them along, and working at the company so I tend to use them instead of my mentor because its not really separated and its not really, I cant really, if I really wanted to, I couldn’t say anything to nasty about the company because but equally, its, even if I do really need time to change, he’s in a position where he can.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK so the buddy system is someone that’s more equal to you rather than a mentor, ok, what do you think the role of a mentor is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm just to keep an eye, someone to hmm get feedback off them about what your doing, how you can do stuff, if you want to do hmm a certain course, if you were thinking about, for your next placement you would like to do this and this and just to bounce ideas from if you need it to get information from.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So is your buddy doing the same sort of work as the mentor then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I think a buddy’s meant to be more so that you know someone in the company you can like, take you to lunch and stuff while you get settled, but because of everyone’s so close and everyone looks after everyone, you can get all the same information out of them, or they’ll tell you who you need to talk to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you think that the mentee has a particular role to play, if that’s a word?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I don’t know, probably just looking for places to be able to sort of develop yourself, its kind of the buzz phrase, personal development at [company], cos’ they have got a learning development centre, spent lots of money on it, as they keep telling us where they do lots of courses and if you want to do a course which isn’t there, they’ll give you a £100 towards the course and things like that if you want to so hmm at least this company is kind of what they want the mentees to be doing. They want them to be looking to develop themselves instead of being told that you should do this and you should do that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK have you ever been given any bad advice by your mentor or buddy?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmmm not yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good. Is there anyone in the company who you think of as a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not really cos’ everyone’s doing such different things, and we’re still kind of learning our way around and even within the company its quite separated because hmm it was such a large company, its like the whole [name] group have only being in [town] for a year cos’ they’ve been in [place] so their kind of linked with everyone else whose had to come up with them and things like that and there’s various places where (inaudible) [town] has adopted everyone. So it’s a bit strange.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what sort of characteristics do you think would make a good role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that’s ok, have you had anyone from university been to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes [name] came up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that your personal tutor or a placement tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He’s my personal tutor and my placement tutor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did he explain what the purpose of the visit was?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm yeah it was just to check that we were following the DIS properly, to check that we weren’t having too many problems, which couldn’t be sorted out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did he speak to your line manager as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK hmm would you be happy to go to him if you did have a problem, any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you in contact with him at other times, can you email him and things like that if you had a problem or would you email anyone else at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm no I generally email [placement tutor] if there’s a problem and he’ll hmmm put me through to ever needs hmm to know about it, to try and sort it out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you know if either the company or the university have a complaints procedures if there were any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I don’t about the university; hmm at work we do have a general complaints procedure, I got a booklet on it (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s a good idea to know about things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm probably, if your having problems its always, even if your not, its nice to know that if you do have problems, there’s somewhere you can go and talk about it and sort it out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok are there appropriate facilities for women at your organisation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (Laughs) yes

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you think of any occasions where you feel like your gender’s determined reactions you’ve got or the outcome of particular events?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not really, the only thing is that all the men there still apologise when they swear but that’s about it, everything else I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah so does that bother you at all when they’re swearing and stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn’t bother me, it annoys me when they feel they have to apologise every time cos’ its kind of, I can swear as well. (Yeah) Not doing anything horrible, just get on with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah ok, do you think that you still want a career in engineering then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will go into the field that you’ve been working in at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm how do you mean what field?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well if the company offered you a job when you graduated would you take it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm yeah I’d kind of like to stay in the defence and just kind of I mean I grew up on [area] where sort of [company] and [company] and the rest of it are based and I’ve kind of had it drummed into me if you were doing engineering you should be working for these people, so I’d kind of like to stay there. Hmmm especially if I ended up doing the same work I’m doing now cos’ I’m really happy with it and find it really interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what sort of role do you think that you would like in the future, do you think you’d like to go into the more managerial or more specialist side of things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I don’t know about specialist cos’ I haven’t done enough places to know (Yeah what…) What I’d like to do, hmm cos’ I feel now if I wanted to be specialist, I’m going to specialise in [name] and its not really thing about [name] or [name]. It’s not really that good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you haven’t got enough experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmmm I’d like to still be involved in projects rather than hmm the managerial aspect because as far as I see, as far up you go, the further you get away from actual engineering you end up probably better off with a business degree or with human resources.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: (Inaudible)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I quite like the distils, have to model stuff up if I have to and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all as a result of doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not really, its kind of firmed up what I want to do cos’ I’ve always wanted to do over research or something hands on and I’d like the idea I’m doing a research based placement. Hmm but and as I said I’ve had bad experience placements before and it has made me sit and think maybe I should just become an accountant, because it has just been sitting there brain numbingly boring, filling in paper work or changing a picture by two millimetres, not really being told where and why, just getting it on the desk and you will do this, and its kind of, I didn’t want to do this, I wanted to do engineering because its meant to be sort of hands on and dealing with this or doing some research and looking at stuff. Hmm so it’s kind of given me confidence back into, it can’t all be like this, it’s just a bad experience and I’ll carry on and it’ll be fine, I’ll do my placements and it will all be fine. It’s kind of done my placement, yeah its great, I definitely want to be here, I’m definitely at the right place, there’s no humming and arring about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah so it’s kind of encouraged you again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work when you finished university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm yeah, it will give me some idea of how I need to operate in a working environment rather than hmm than what I do at uni and just be sort of used to the, that routine and knowing that its all right to know that you need these equations but you’ve got to be able to apply them for this and while your applying it to that, that maybe the optimal answer for that, you need to build it which you can’t do with this and things like that. So just knowing the whole process and I mean if I do end up going back to the same company, it gives me a head start, cos’ I’ll know people there, I already know that if I need help with this, I can go and talk to Mike, or I can talk to John if I need things so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there any way they could make the course more about the whole process and more hands on?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not really cos’ of, well I don’t know about the second year, where they could probably do more project base work which I know they do anyway, but I mean I don’t know whether it was industrial type project or here’s a work bench, here’s a thousand pounds, build this and sort it out and write a report. Hmm but I don’t think they could in the first year because there’s just so much theory to learn about the background of everything. If you try to make it fit together with a more industrial kind of feel, you never get as much information across, hmm

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend other students do a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it should be compulsory?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No because hmm I know a few people who, they’ve decided to carry on with the degree for various reasons, I mean some of them just want to be out of university so they don’t have a stall in their studying, or they’ve taken a year out before they’ve come to uni and don’t want to lose any more time, don’t want to sort of finish and be twice as long to everyone else in university. Hmm as well as people who have done placements before they’ve come here and already know, I think its just kind of the in thing about how, how do you learn and whether you need to sort of know for sure that you want to be on this degree and all the rest of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK I’ve just got a couple of questions to ask you which I asked you in your last interview to see if your opinion has changed since working in the industry. What five words would you now use to describe your field of engineering? … Shall I tell you what you said last time and see if you still agree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said that it was routed in old ways and well established.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm don’t know

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you still agree with that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s a bit strange, never mind.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you now think that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm not really, you’ve just got to get used to, well its more not you getting used to it, its everyone else getting used to you. Hmm it’s more just being able to get on where, sort of guys who have been working their for 30 years and haven’t worked with a girl before. Most of them, their all right, some of them a bit strange about it, just because they are not used to it and sometimes they feel they’ve got to be nice to you and all the rest of it. But as long as you sort of stay acting like you normally act and all the rest of it then they normally get the message that you aren’t to be treated with kitten gloves and all the rest of it, you can do as much as they can, its all fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, have your colleagues taken a while to get used to you then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm where I am at the moment, not many people are too bothered, but hmm a lot of the graduates are working with [name] at the moment which is a fairly young team as the company goes and hmm I mean the [name] guys, they don’t teach, they all have teenage daughters and their all about my age and their all (inaudible), get on with it, we know you can do x, y and z, you know you can be as stroppy as anyone else, as long as you don’t sort of go out there thinking that your going to get special treatment or try and get special treatment, its all fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you think that it is an issue that there are say fewer women than men there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think its become an issue because people have suddenly noticed, hmm in my mind I’ve never seen it as when people have said but you’re a girl, it’s a bit of a strange degree. Its like, I wanted to take the degree, I was interested in it so I’m becoming an engineer. It’s never been kind of, what can I do to, cos’ it will be strange, sort of, I’ll go and be an engineer. I’ve never seen that, its kind of like, yes I’ve done physics and all the rest of it, so I’m doing this, the same way my friends did this and decided they wanted to be doctors or chemistry students, there’s, I just don’t see why its become so (inaudible), its only become a big deal because they’ve looked at their statistics and gone, do you realise that only like 2% of them are women, its like, does it matter as long as the jobs get done and no ones been turned away on purpose because of it. If there’s like actual discrimination, to say no, we only employ blokes, that’s fine, there’s an issue there, but with the whole industry as an employer of women, why does it need to employ women, it needs to employ engineers. (Yeah) So I’m not really into the getting more women into engineering, I’ve always been, if I’ve done stuff with schools and stuff, I don’t mind helping them getting into science and maths and sort of take that kind of route, but in the end I’m not gonna say, oh you really like physics, your good at maths well, come and do engineering, you don’t want to do physics, you don’t want to do anything else, you don’t want to go off and be a doctor, come and do engineering cos’ its great. I’d much rather say well if you like it, get on with it and have a look at what you can do because I don’t see the point in suddenly going, you’ve kind of got the right things, you do want to do this because we need to boost the numbers for whatever reasons.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that’s great. Just one last thing, you mentioned that another team was much younger than, do you think when people aren’t used to maybe having women to work with, that there is an age issue there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm I don’t think its so much an age issue, its just what people are used to hmm I mean at lancing, where I did my first placement while I was at A levels hmm although I wasn’t working on the shop floor, I spent a lot of time around fitters, and when they haven’t been around hmm working with women and stuff, they found it quite hard to adjust, but they were kind of more asking lots of questions about why you were there rather than making it any harder for you or anything and stuff. (Yeah) Hmm but then again here, where people from, where people have graduated recently with more women in classes, their fine with that, their used to working with it or at the other end of the scale within my group where there’s people, they’ve got their kids which are as old as I am and know that sort of we’re not going to be (inaudible) and all the rest of it and we don’t need treating with kitten gloves, we can just get on with it, and then there’s people whose sort of have worked a lot with people in HR where it’s the complete reverse, where there’s hundreds of women, not many blokes and their fine with it. But you’ve got people who have come up various companies and they’ve never had any women it’s a bit of a culture shock some of them. Its, its just getting used to things, if you suddenly sort of, I mean I know going from an all girls school in sixth form we were suddenly joined with [school] and it was odd having classes with blokes but after the first month or so you got used to it. (Yeah) It’s just sort of…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Making more (inaudible)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that’s everything, thank you very much.
